claim: Six adult rats were implanted with either microwire electrode arrays (n=5) or custom-built high-density silicon probes (n=1) in the primary motor cortex (M1) and the dorsolateral striatum (DLS).
source: We implanted six adult rats with either microwire electrode arrays (n=5) or custom-built high-density silicon probes (Egert et al., 2020) (n=1) in the primary motor cortex (M1) and the dorsolateral striatum (DLS), which receives the majority of M1 projections to the striatum (Figure 1a; Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Aoki et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number and type of implants in specific brain regions.

claim: The DLS receives the majority of M1 projections to the striatum.
source: We implanted six adult rats with either microwire electrode arrays (n=5) or custom-built high-density silicon probes (Egert et al., 2020) (n=1) in the primary motor cortex (M1) and the dorsolateral striatum (DLS), which receives the majority of M1 projections to the striatum (Figure 1a; Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Aoki et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Aoki et al., 2019 and reference to Figure 1a showing anterograde tracing.

claim: Neural activity in M1 and DLS was simultaneously monitored as rats underwent long-term reach-to-grasp skill training ranging from 5 to 14 days.
source: Neural activity in both regions was simultaneously monitored as rats underwent long-term reach-to-grasp skill training (range: 5–14 days).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the experimental design and duration.

claim: On each training day, rats were recorded during a 2-3 hr pre-training period, a 100-150 trial training period, and a 2-3 hr post-training period.
source: On each day, rats were placed in a custom-built behavioral box (Wong et al., 2015) and neural activity was recorded during a 2–3 hr pre-training period (consisting of both sleep and wake periods), a 100–150 trial training period, and a second 2–3 hr post-training period (Figure 1b; pre-training period length: 154.1±6.1 min, post-training period length: 159.4±5.4 min, mean± SEM, n=56 days).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific timing and trial numbers for the experimental protocol.

claim: Pre-training period length averaged 154.1±6.1 min and post-training period length averaged 159.4±5.4 min (mean±SEM, n=56 days).
source: On each day, rats were placed in a custom-built behavioral box (Wong et al., 2015) and neural activity was recorded during a 2–3 hr pre-training period (consisting of both sleep and wake periods), a 100–150 trial training period, and a second 2–3 hr post-training period (Figure 1b; pre-training period length: 154.1±6.1 min, post-training period length: 159.4±5.4 min, mean± SEM, n=56 days).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative measurements of recording period durations.

claim: Behavioral states (wake, NREM, and REM) were classified using cortical LFP power and movement measured from video or EMG activity.
source: During pre- and post-training periods, behavioral states—wake and sleep (NREM and REM) —were classified using standard methods based on cortical local field potential (LFP) power and movement measured from video or electromyography (EMG) activity (Watson et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript describes the methodology for behavioral state classification with citation to Watson et al., 2016.

claim: A consistent day-to-day velocity profile emerged within the first 8 days of training.
source: Comparing the trial-averaged velocity profile on each day of training to the trial-averaged velocity profile on the last day of training, which served as a learned 'template,' revealed that a consistent day-to-day velocity profile emerged within the first 8 days of training (Figure 1d; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the timeframe for emergence of consistent velocity profiles, supported by figures.

claim: Single-trial peak reaching velocity increased across training days and correlated with the consistency of the velocity profile (r=0.55, P=5×10−5).
source: Single-trial peak reaching velocity also generally increased across training days, correlated to the consistency of the velocity profile (Figure 1—figure supplement 3; r=0.55, P=5×10−5, Pearson's r), consistent with previous work suggesting that movement speed is a relevant aspect of skill learning (Lemke et al., 2019; Hikosaka et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific correlation statistics and references supporting figures.

claim: Movement speed is a relevant aspect of skill learning.
source: Single-trial peak reaching velocity also generally increased across training days, correlated to the consistency of the velocity profile (Figure 1—figure supplement 3; r=0.55, P=5×10−5, Pearson's r), consistent with previous work suggesting that movement speed is a relevant aspect of skill learning (Lemke et al., 2019; Hikosaka et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Lemke et al., 2019; Hikosaka et al., 2013).

claim: Six rats were trained for 10 days with infusions of either 1 µl of NMDA receptor antagonist AP5 (5 µg/µl) or saline into DLS immediately after training on each day.
source: We trained a new cohort of animals (n=six rats) for 10 days, infusing either 1 µl of NMDA receptor antagonist AP5 (5 µg/µl) or saline into DLS immediately after training on each day (Figure 1e).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the experimental design for the infusion study.

claim: Day-to-day changes in velocity profile correlation were significantly decreased with AP5 infusions compared to saline infusions (P=8×10−3) or changes observed in the learning cohort (P=0.48).
source: This revealed that offline striatal NMDA activation was important for skill learning, as day-to-day changes in velocity profile correlation were significantly decreased with AP5 infusions, compared to saline infusions or changes observed in the learning cohort (Figure 1f; Figure 1—figure supplement 4; n=six rats with AP5 infusions, −0.11±0.06 total correlation value change, mean± SEM, n=six rats with saline infusions, 0.16±0.06 total correlation value change, n=six rats in learning cohort, 0.25±0.08 total correlation value change; AP5 infusions vs. saline infusions: P=8×10−3, Wilcoxon rank-sum test, AP5 infusions vs. learning cohort: P=0.48, Wilcoxon rank-sum test, saline infusions vs. learning cohort: P=2×10−3, Wilcoxon rank-sum test; for all animals, the last day of training which served as template was excluded from total correlation value change calculation).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific statistical comparisons with P values.

claim: Offline striatal NMDA activation is important for skill learning.
source: This revealed that offline striatal NMDA activation was important for skill learning, as day-to-day changes in velocity profile correlation were significantly decreased with AP5 infusions, compared to saline infusions or changes observed in the learning cohort (Figure 1f; Figure 1—figure supplement 4; n=six rats with AP5 infusions, −0.11±0.06 total correlation value change, mean± SEM, n=six rats with saline infusions, 0.16±0.06 total correlation value change, n=six rats in learning cohort, 0.25±0.08 total correlation value change; AP5 infusions vs. saline infusions: P=8×10−3, Wilcoxon rank-sum test, AP5 infusions vs. learning cohort: P=0.48, Wilcoxon rank-sum test, saline infusions vs. learning cohort: P=2×10−3, Wilcoxon rank-sum test; for all animals, the last day of training which served as template was excluded from total correlation value change calculation).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data showing effects of AP5 infusions.

claim: 4-8 Hz LFP coherence was calculated across each M1 and DLS electrode during each pre- and post-training period throughout learning during NREM.
source: To measure functional connectivity we calculated 4–8 Hz LFP coherence across each M1 and DLS electrode during each pre- and post-training period throughout learning, as LFP signals in the theta frequency band have been previously shown to reflect corticostriatal spiking activity (Lemke et al., 2019; Koralek et al., 2013; Thorn and Graybiel, 2014). We calculated coherence specifically during NREM to establish a consistent measure of functional connectivity across days (Figure 2a).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the methodology for measuring functional connectivity.

claim: LFP signals in the theta frequency band have been previously shown to reflect corticostriatal spiking activity.
source: To measure functional connectivity we calculated 4–8 Hz LFP coherence across each M1 and DLS electrode during each pre- and post-training period throughout learning, as LFP signals in the theta frequency band have been previously shown to reflect corticostriatal spiking activity (Lemke et al., 2019; Koralek et al., 2013; Thorn and Graybiel, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The phase difference between M1 and DLS 4-8 Hz LFP signals during NREM was inconsistent with volume conduction.
source: This resulted in a phase difference between M1 and DLS 4–8 Hz LFP signals during NREM that was inconsistent with volume conduction (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding with reference to supporting figure.

claim: M1 electrodes with high LFP coherence with DLS electrodes entrained DLS units to a greater degree than M1 electrodes with low LFP coherence with DLS electrodes.
source: We found that M1 electrodes with high LFP coherence with DLS electrodes also entrained DLS units to a greater degree than M1 electrodes with low LFP coherence with DLS electrodes (Figure 2e and f).

source: We found a significant relationship between the emergence of a consistent skilled action and mean LFP coherence measured during the pre-training period for frequencies between ~5 and 11 Hz (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), indicating that offline LFP coherence in the theta frequency range uniquely reflects network changes relevant to learning.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding with reference to supporting figure.

source: We found a significant relationship between the emergence of a consistent skilled action and mean LFP coherence measured during the pre-training period for frequencies between ~5 and 11 Hz (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), indicating that offline LFP coherence in the theta frequency range uniquely reflects network changes relevant to learning.

source: Across animals, mean changes in 4–8 Hz LFP coherence occurring online were not significantly different than zero, while changes occurring offline were skewed positive (Figure 3d; online LFP coherence changes: t(1413)=−0.34, P=0.73, offline LFP coherence changes: t(1413)=23.4, P=7×10−103 one-sample t-test).

evidence: The manuscript provides specific statistical test results.

source: Notably, there was a close relationship between 4–8 Hz LFP coherence measured during the pre-training period on each day and consistency in skilled action execution during the subsequent training period (Figure 3e; r=0.73, P=5×10−10, Pearson's r), indicating that offline increases in corticostriatal functional connectivity closely tracked skill learning.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific correlation statistics.

claim: Offline increases in corticostriatal functional connectivity closely tracked skill learning.
source: Notably, there was a close relationship between 4–8 Hz LFP coherence measured during the pre-training period on each day and consistency in skilled action execution during the subsequent training period (Figure 3e; r=0.73, P=5×10−10, Pearson's r), indicating that offline increases in corticostriatal functional connectivity closely tracked skill learning.

source: We found that the ability to predict DLS neural trajectories during execution of the reaching action increased with training, while the ability to predict the trajectory representations of DLS activity during a baseline, non-reaching, period did not significantly change (Figure 4b; action execution: 0.18±0.05 Pearson's r on first 3 training days (average of three correlation values corresponding to top three PCs) and 0.40±0.04 Pearson's r on last 3 training days, P=7×10−3, Wilcoxon rank-sum test, n=11 early and late days, only days with greater than 6 M1 and DLS units recorded were considered; baseline period: 0.03±0.02 Pearson's r on first 3 training days and 0.02±0.02 Pearson's r on last 3 training days, P=0.28, Wilcoxon rank-sum test, n=11 early and late days, only days with greater than 6 M1 and DLS units recorded were considered).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific statistical comparisons between early and late training.

claim: The ability to predict DLS neural trajectories during a baseline, non-reaching period did not significantly change with training (P=0.28).
source: We found that the ability to predict DLS neural trajectories during execution of the reaching action increased with training, while the ability to predict the trajectory representations of DLS activity during a baseline, non-reaching, period did not significantly change (Figure 4b; action execution: 0.18±0.05 Pearson's r on first 3 training days (average of three correlation values corresponding to top three PCs) and 0.40±0.04 Pearson's r on last 3 training days, P=7×10−3, Wilcoxon rank-sum test, n=11 early and late days, only days with greater than 6 M1 and DLS units recorded were considered; baseline period: 0.03±0.02 Pearson's r on first 3 training days and 0.02±0.02 Pearson's r on last 3 training days, P=0.28, Wilcoxon rank-sum test, n=11 early and late days, only days with greater than 6 M1 and DLS units recorded were considered).

claim: There was no significant difference in the trial-averaged spiking modulation of DLS units during action execution between early and late training days (P=0.09).
source: However, we found no significant difference in the trial-averaged spiking modulation of DLS units during action execution between early (first 3 days of training) and late (last 3 days of training) training days (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; 1.6±0.05 modulation value on early days and 1.7±0.09 modulation value on late days, mean± SEM, t(409)=−1.7, P=0.09, two-sample t-test, n=233 DLS units on early days and 178 DLS units on late days), as well as no significant difference in the variance explained by the first three PCs computed from DLS activity during action execution between early and late training days (58.0±2.7 variance explained on early days and 52.2±3.0 on late days, mean± SEM, t(27)=1.4, P=0.17, two-sample t-test, n=17 early days and 12 late days).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific statistical test results comparing early and late training.

claim: There was no significant difference in the variance explained by the first three PCs computed from DLS activity during action execution between early and late training days (P=0.17).
source: However, we found no significant difference in the trial-averaged spiking modulation of DLS units during action execution between early (first 3 days of training) and late (last 3 days of training) training days (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; 1.6±0.05 modulation value on early days and 1.7±0.09 modulation value on late days, mean± SEM, t(409)=−1.7, P=0.09, two-sample t-test, n=233 DLS units on early days and 178 DLS units on late days), as well as no significant difference in the variance explained by the first three PCs computed from DLS activity during action execution between early and late training days (58.0±2.7 variance explained on early days and 52.2±3.0 on late days, mean± SEM, t(27)=1.4, P=0.17, two-sample t-test, n=17 early days and 12 late days).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific statistical test results.

claim: The increased ability to predict DLS neural trajectories during skill execution from M1 spiking activity reflects cross-area dynamics emerging with learning, rather than local learning-related changes in DLS.
source: Altogether, these results provide evidence that the increased ability to predict DLS neural trajectories during skill execution from M1 spiking activity reflects cross-area dynamics emerging with learning, rather than local learning-related changes in DLS.

claim: 4-8 Hz LFP coherence measured during the pre-training period on each day was significantly correlated to the ability to predict DLS neural trajectories during the subsequent training period from M1 spiking activity (r=0.58, P=9×10−4).
source: Consistent with the idea that offline plasticity in the corticostriatal network is relevant to skill learning, we found that 4–8 Hz LFP coherence measured during the pre-training period on each day was significantly correlated to the ability to predict DLS neural trajectories during the subsequent training period from M1 spiking activity (Figure 4c; reaching period: r=0.58, P=9×10−4, Pearson's r, baseline period: r=0.03, P=0.87).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific correlation statistics.

claim: Approximately 2.6% of M1 and DLS neuron pairs (311/12,169 pairs) had a significant short-latency spiking relationship.
source: Across the population of recorded M1 (n=1100 units) and DLS neurons (n=579 units, 71% classified as medium spiny neurons [MSNs] based on spike width; Figure 5—figure supplement 1), we identified ~2.6% of pairs with a significant short-latency spiking relationship (311/12,169 pairs; Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages and numbers of neuron pairs.

claim: 71% of recorded DLS neurons were classified as medium spiny neurons (MSNs) based on spike width.
source: Across the population of recorded M1 (n=1100 units) and DLS neurons (n=579 units, 71% classified as medium spiny neurons [MSNs] based on spike width; Figure 5—figure supplement 1), we identified ~2.6% of pairs with a significant short-latency spiking relationship (311/12,169 pairs; Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific classification percentages.

claim: Convergent activation from several cortical neurons is likely required to drive MSN spiking activity.
source: This is consistent with recent work that carefully dissected the relationship between cortical and striatal activity and observed broad cross-correlation histograms with peaks at a short-latency delay (~3 ms) between cortical and striatal spiking activity (Peters et al., 2021). The relatively broad cross-correlation histogram peaks observed between M1 and DLS neurons, compared to those typically seen between cortical neurons (Fujisawa et al., 2008), may be because striatal MSNs receive weak input from many cortical neurons, rather than strong input from individual cortical neurons (Dudman and Gerfen, 2015). Therefore, convergent activation from several cortical neurons is likely required to drive MSN spiking activity, resulting in temporal jitter that decreases the consistency of any specific M1 and DLS neuron spiking relationship.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and reasoning about MSN connectivity.

claim: Corticostriatal transmission was higher during NREM compared to wake in 77% of coupled M1 and DLS neuron pairs.
source: We found that corticostriatal transmission was higher during NREM, compared to wake, in 77% of coupled M1 and DLS neuron pairs (Figure 5c), suggesting activity patterns in NREM may be particularly relevant for offline corticostriatal plasticity given the increased transmission of activity from M1 to DLS.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages of neuron pairs showing this pattern.

claim: Activity patterns in NREM may be particularly relevant for offline corticostriatal plasticity given the increased transmission of activity from M1 to DLS.
source: We found that corticostriatal transmission was higher during NREM, compared to wake, in 77% of coupled M1 and DLS neuron pairs (Figure 5c), suggesting activity patterns in NREM may be particularly relevant for offline corticostriatal plasticity given the increased transmission of activity from M1 to DLS.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data on NREM transmission strength.

claim: Both LFP signals and spiking in DLS were significantly modulated during slow oscillations, delta waves, and sleep spindles detected in M1.
source: We found that both LFP signals and spiking in DLS were significantly modulated during SOs, delta waves, and sleep spindles detected in M1 (Figure 5e; Figure 5—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding with reference to supporting figures.

claim: Corticostriatal transmission strength was greatest during sleep spindles, compared to slow oscillations or delta waves.
source: This revealed that corticostriatal transmission strength was greatest during sleep spindles, compared to SOs or delta waves (Figure 5f), suggesting that sleep spindles during NREM may be particularly relevant periods for activity-dependent plasticity within the corticostriatal network.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this comparison with reference to supporting figure.

claim: Sleep spindles during NREM may be particularly relevant periods for activity-dependent plasticity within the corticostriatal network.
source: This revealed that corticostriatal transmission strength was greatest during sleep spindles, compared to SOs or delta waves (Figure 5f), suggesting that sleep spindles during NREM may be particularly relevant periods for activity-dependent plasticity within the corticostriatal network.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data on transmission strength during different NREM rhythms.

claim: Corticostriatal functional connectivity was specifically preserved in spindle-modulated neuron pairs during the post-training period, in contrast to non-spindle modulated pairs during the post-training period or all pairs during the pre-training period.
source: This revealed that corticostriatal functional connectivity, measured by short-latency cross-correlation magnitude, was specifically preserved in spindle-modulated neuron pairs during the post-training period, in contrast to non-spindle modulated pairs during the post-training period or all pairs during the pre-training period (Figure 6b and c).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this pattern with reference to supporting figures.

claim: Sleep spindles following training may be involved in preserving learning-related cross-area connectivity in the corticostriatal network.
source: This suggested that sleep spindles following training may be involved in preserving learning-related cross-area connectivity in the corticostriatal network.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data on spindle-modulated neuron pairs.

claim: Post-training period changes in short-latency cross-correlation magnitude averaged across coupled M1 and DLS neuron pairs were significantly correlated to subsequent overnight changes in 4-8 Hz LFP coherence averaged across M1 and DLS electrodes.
source: Strikingly, post-training period changes in short-latency cross-correlation magnitude averaged across coupled M1 and DLS neuron pairs were significantly correlated to subsequent overnight changes in 4–8 Hz LFP coherence averaged across M1 and DLS electrodes (Figure 6d), indicating that sleep-spindle related preservation of corticostriatal functional connectivity within the first few hours after training may be related to overnight plasticity in the corticostriatal network.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this correlation with reference to supporting figure.

claim: Sleep-spindle related preservation of corticostriatal functional connectivity within the first few hours after training may be related to overnight plasticity in the corticostriatal network.
source: Strikingly, post-training period changes in short-latency cross-correlation magnitude averaged across coupled M1 and DLS neuron pairs were significantly correlated to subsequent overnight changes in 4–8 Hz LFP coherence averaged across M1 and DLS electrodes (Figure 6d), indicating that sleep-spindle related preservation of corticostriatal functional connectivity within the first few hours after training may be related to overnight plasticity in the corticostriatal network.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation data.

claim: There was a large shift in the temporal proximity to preceding slow oscillations from the pre- to post-training period, with a larger proportion of sleep spindles in the post-training period 'nested' near slow oscillations (P=6×10−39).
source: We found a large shift in the temporal proximity to preceding SOs from the pre- to post-training period, with a larger proportion of sleep spindles in the post-training period 'nested' near SOs (Figure 7a; P=6×10−39, two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test).

claim: Corticostriatal transmission strength was significantly elevated after slow oscillation-nested sleep spindles compared to non-SO-nested sleep spindles.
source: We found that corticostriatal transmission strength, measured by short-latency cross-correlation magnitude, was significantly elevated after slow oscillation-nested sleep spindles (SO-nested spindles; sleep spindles within 1 s of a SO) compared to non-SO-nested sleep spindles (Figure 7b; non-SO-nested spindles; sleep spindles occurring at least 5 s after a SO).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this comparison with reference to supporting figure.

claim: Increased nesting of slow oscillations and sleep spindles may account for the unique preservation of corticostriatal functional connectivity within spindle-modulated M1 and DLS neuron pairs during the post-training period.
source: This suggested that increased nesting of SOs and sleep spindles may account for the unique preservation of corticostriatal functional connectivity within spindle-modulated M1 and DLS neuron pairs during the post-training period.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data on SO-nested spindles.

claim: NREM sleep is a relevant period for corticostriatal plasticity during skill learning.
source: Here, we monitor the corticostriatal network throughout long-term skill learning in rats and find that non-rapid-eye-movement (NREM) sleep is a relevant period for corticostriatal plasticity.
evidence: This is a main conclusion stated in the abstract.

claim: The offline activation of striatal NMDA receptors is required for skill learning.
source: We first show that the offline activation of striatal NMDA receptors is required for skill learning.
evidence: This is a main finding stated in the abstract.

claim: Corticostriatal functional connectivity increases offline, coupled to emerging consistent skilled movements and coupled cross-area neural dynamics.
source: We then show that corticostriatal functional connectivity increases offline, coupled to emerging consistent skilled movements, and coupled cross-area neural dynamics.
evidence: This is a main finding stated in the abstract.

claim: NREM sleep spindles are uniquely poised to mediate corticostriatal plasticity through interactions with slow oscillations.
source: We then identify NREM sleep spindles as uniquely poised to mediate corticostriatal plasticity, through interactions with slow oscillations.

source: Our results provide evidence that sleep shapes cross-area coupling required for skill learning.

claim: The strength of cortical connectivity to the striatum influences the balance between behavioral variability and stability.
source: The strength of cortical connectivity to the striatum influences the balance between behavioral variability and stability.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as background knowledge.

claim: Learning to consistently produce a skilled action requires plasticity in corticostriatal connectivity associated with repeated training of the action.
source: Learning to consistently produce a skilled action requires plasticity in corticostriatal connectivity associated with repeated training of the action.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as background knowledge.

claim: Cortical and basal ganglia circuits regulate behavioral variability, as evidenced in habit development, skill learning, and the pathophysiology of neuropsychiatric disorders.
source: Cortical and basal ganglia circuits regulate behavioral variability, as evidenced in habit development (Gremel et al., 2016; O'Hare et al., 2016; Rueda-Orozco and Robbe, 2015; Malvaez and Wassum, 2018; Lipton et al., 2019; Yin and Knowlton, 2006), skill learning (Santos et al., 2015; Kupferschmidt et al., 2017; Koralek et al., 2012; Yin et al., 2009), as well as the pathophysiology of neuropsychiatric disorders such as obsessive-compulsive disorder and autism spectrum disorder (Vicente et al., 2020; Shepherd, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The ability to consistently produce a skilled action is accompanied by emerging coordinated neural activity across the motor cortex and striatum during action execution.
source: In the case of skill learning, the ability to consistently produce a skilled action is accompanied by emerging coordinated neural activity across the motor cortex and striatum during action execution (Santos et al., 2015; Lemke et al., 2019; Koralek et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Skill learning has been associated with striatal NMDA receptor activation.
source: Skill learning has also been associated with striatal NMDA receptor activation (Santos et al., 2015; Koralek et al., 2012; Jin and Costa, 2010; Dang et al., 2006), suggesting that the activity-dependent potentiation of cortical inputs to the striatum may be required (Calabresi et al., 1992; Charpier and Deniau, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Activity-dependent potentiation of cortical inputs to the striatum may be required for skill learning.
source: Skill learning has also been associated with striatal NMDA receptor activation (Santos et al., 2015; Koralek et al., 2012; Jin and Costa, 2010; Dang et al., 2006), suggesting that the activity-dependent potentiation of cortical inputs to the striatum may be required (Calabresi et al., 1992; Charpier and Deniau, 1997).
evidence: This is a speculation based on cited work about NMDA receptors and potentiation.

claim: Reactivations of training-related neural activity patterns during sleep promote motor skill learning.
source: This possibility is motivated by evidence that 'reactivations' of training-related neural activity patterns during sleep promote motor skill learning (Yang et al., 2014; Ramanathan et al., 2015; Gulati et al., 2014; Kim et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Both cortical and subcortical brain areas are engaged during the sleep-dependent consolidation of motor skills.
source: Moreover, it has been proposed that both cortical and subcortical brain areas are engaged during the sleep-dependent consolidation of motor skills (Vahdat et al., 2017; Boutin et al., 2018; Doyon et al., 2018; Doyon and Benali, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

source: While sleep spindles have been previously linked to plasticity (Durkin et al., 2017; Barakat et al., 2013; Rosanova and Ulrich, 2005; Clawson et al., 2016), how neural activity during sleep spindles leads to long-term plasticity remains unclear.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Slow oscillation and sleep spindle activity patterns can drive NMDA receptor-dependent potentiation in vitro.
source: It has been demonstrated in vitro that SO and sleep spindle activity patterns can drive NMDA receptor-dependent potentiation (Rosanova and Ulrich, 2005; Chauvette et al., 2012).

claim: There is evidence for NMDA receptor-dependent potentiation of cortical inputs to the striatum during skill learning.
source: Given evidence for NMDA receptor-dependent potentiation of cortical inputs to the striatum during skill learning (Calabresi et al., 1992; Charpier and Deniau, 1997), one intriguing possibility is that sleep spindles, gated by their temporal proximity to preceding SOs, promote the potentiation of cortical inputs to the striatum through NMDA receptor activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Sleep spindles, gated by their temporal proximity to preceding slow oscillations, may promote the potentiation of cortical inputs to the striatum through NMDA receptor activation.

claim: The synaptic homeostasis hypothesis proposes that sleep drives the general homeostatic downscaling of synapses which are upregulated during wake.
source: We also observed a decrement in short-latency spike-timing relationships within M1 and DLS neuron pairs measured in pre-training sleep, or pairs measured in post-training sleep but not modulated during sleep spindles. This change is consistent with a growing body of work supporting the synaptic homeostasis hypothesis (SHY), which proposes that sleep drives the general homeostatic downscaling of synapses which are upregulated during wake (Tononi and Cirelli, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tononi and Cirelli, 2014.

claim: General downscaling during sleep can support memory consolidation indirectly by increasing the signal-to-noise of memory representations encoded during wake.

claim: Activity during sleep may preserve activity patterns generated during learning while also downscaling task-irrelevant activity.
source: Recent work suggests a way to reconcile both ideas, demonstrating that activity during sleep may preserve activity patterns generated during learning while also downscaling task-irrelevant activity (Kim et al., 2019; Gulati et al., 2017).

claim: NREM sleep rhythms have been linked to both preservation/strengthening and downscaling processes.
source: As NREM sleep rhythms have been linked to both processes (Kim et al., 2019; Huber et al., 2004; Gulati et al., 2017; Norimoto et al., 2018), it will be important to explore how NREM rhythms differentially impact downscaling versus preserving/strengthening synapses for nearby neurons in the same brain region or connected neurons across different brain regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Increased coordination of M1 and DLS neural activity with skill acquisition has been previously shown.
source: Here, we show that 4–8 Hz LFP coherence across M1 and DLS measured during NREM closely tracks the emergence of a stable skilled reaching behavior, as measured by the emergence of a stable day-to-day reaching velocity profile. This is consistent with previous work showing increased coordination of M1 and DLS neural activity with skill acquisition (Santos et al., 2015; Lemke et al., 2019; Koralek et al., 2013), suggesting that increased communication and connectivity between cortex and striatum may be a central feature of stable skilled behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Increased communication and connectivity between cortex and striatum may be a central feature of stable skilled behavior.

claim: Sleep benefits speed and consistency in motor tasks in humans and rodents.

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies in humans and rodents.

claim: The basal ganglia are an important regulator of movement vigor.

claim: Neural signals across cortex and striatum grow more coordinated during skill learning.

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

source: One intriguing possibility is that the nature of corticostriatal communication evolves during learning.
